The eggs of the Little penguin (Eudyptula minor) are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] for a period that has been precisely documented in captive colonies, with hatching occurring 36 days [ab = 36 days] after laying. This incubation duration is somewhat shorter than that of larger spheniscids, likely reflecting the constraints of a smaller body mass on egg temperature regulation and the reduced thermal inertia of the nest chamber. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling emerges at a remarkably modest body mass of only 80 grams [Wwb = 80 grams], a value that underscores the substantial energetic investment still required from the provisioning adults. This neonatal mass constitutes a relatively small fraction of the species' ultimate adult size, highlighting a developmental strategy that prioritizes an early transition to exogenous feeding under the thermal protection of the brood patch. The initial chick is sparsely downed and entirely dependent on the parents for both thermoregulation and food delivery.

During the subsequent rapid growth phase, the developing chick is subject to the prevailing thermal conditions of the burrow, which typically reflect the adult core temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] during brooding bouts. Under this regime, the nestling attains the developmental milestone of fledging after 62 days since birth [tx = 62 days since birth] at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This fledging age, roughly two months post-hatching, is characteristic of a semi-precocial trajectory common among smaller penguins, where the chick must achieve nearly adult-like thermoregulatory capacity and feather development before departing the nest. Throughout this period, the chick experiences a dramatic increase in mass, eventually reaching a plateau that defines the onset of its independent life. Fledglings depart with a body composition that must sustain them through the challenging transition to self-feeding at sea.

Sexual maturation in this species is not achieved until well after the fledgling has mastered foraging skills and built sufficient body reserves. The attainment of puberty, marking the onset of gonadal development and the potential for reproductive activity, is recorded at approximately 186 days since birth [tp = approximately 186 days since birth] under the consistently warm conditions of the burrow environment, which remains near the adult body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This relatively extended juvenile period, spanning over six months, likely reflects the time required for the immature individual to perfect underwater hunting techniques and to accumulate the substantial lipid stores necessary to survive the energetic costs of the molt and the subsequent breeding season. Young birds during this sub-adult phase are often observed in creches or foraging in small groups along the coast of southern Australia and New Zealand.

The first breeding attempt is a significant energetic commitment, and it is deferred until the individual has fully matured. The age at first successful reproduction, or time since birth at first brood, has been documented at 2 years [tR = 2 years] for individuals reared under optimal conditions. at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]This two-year delay before entering the breeding population is common among long-lived seabirds and is interpreted as a life-history strategy to maximize lifetime reproductive output by ensuring that only physiologically robust adults attempt to raise young. The first nesting effort often occurs in a simple burrow or rock crevice, and the clutch typically consists of a clutch of two chicks per clutch [N_R_i = two chicks per clutch] and a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with occasional replacement clutches if the first is lost early in incubation.

Long-term banding studies have revealed that the maximum lifespan of the Little penguin in the wild can approach 20 years [am = 20 years], an impressive longevity for such a small seabird, all the while maintaining a core body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. With a typical annual reproductive output limited to a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] comprising two chicks per clutch [N_R_i = two chicks per clutch], the lifetime reproductive output is constrained by this slow pace of replacement. The ultimate wet weight of a mature adult, representing the maximum body mass attained, typically stabilizes around 1232 grams [Wwi = around 1232 grams], though individuals frequently exhibit seasonal fluctuations in mass related to molt and provisioning demands. This modest adult size, combined with a remarkably long reproductive window, underscores the species' adaptation to a stable marine environment where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity.
